stimulus.text: The engraving, 'The town of Boston in New England and British ships of war landing their troops! 1768,' shows Boston harbor crowded with British warships. Small boats ferry red-coated soldiers ashore, and columns of troops march in formation along the wharf while the town's church steeples rise behind them.
stimulus.source_note: Engraved by Paul Revere, published 1770 (the landing shown is 1768). Library of Congress. Public domain (pre-1930).

source: original; stimulus viewed before writing — by Paul Revere, published 1770, Library of Congress, public domain.

books.section: A. Colonial Resistance to British Policies in the Aftermath of the French and Indian War
The Sugar Act, the Currency Act, and the Stamp Act

stem: Which of the following best explains why the presence of these troops increased tensions in Boston?

options.text: The soldiers refused to protect the town from French attack
options.misconception: There was no French threat to Boston in 1768 — the French had been driven from the continent in 1763, and the troops were there to enforce British laws, not to fight France.

options.text: The soldiers took Bostonians' jobs and symbolized British repression
The soldiers demanded that Bostonians house them in their own bedrooms
options.misconception: The Quartering Act housed soldiers in barracks and, when those filled, in inns and public houses — not in colonists' bedrooms, and the job competition mattered more than the housing.

options.text: The soldiers closed the town's churches and banned public worship
options.misconception: No church was closed and worship was never banned — the troops enforced customs laws, and the anger came from jobs and from the sight of an army in peacetime.

rationales.B: Background: the troops took part-time waterfront work that Bostonians needed, and their very presence — a standing army in a peacetime town — struck colonists as a threat to liberty. Jobs and symbolism together made the soldiers hated.
rationales.A: France was gone from the continent by 1763. There was no French attack to protect Boston from.
rationales.C: Bedrooms were never demanded. Barracks and public houses held the troops; the real friction was jobs.
rationales.D: Worship was never touched. The troops enforced customs laws — the anger was about work and about an army in peacetime.
rationales.general:
1. Ask what the soldiers did off duty. They took part-time work on the waterfront — work Bostonians needed for themselves.
2. Ask what the soldiers meant on duty. A standing army in a peacetime town, which colonists had long seen as a threat to liberty.
3. Put the two together. The troops cost Bostonians both wages and the feeling of freedom — an economic grievance wearing a political uniform.
Remember: resentment grows fastest when one grievance is really two — look for the second one hiding behind the first.
